speaker: SPEAKER_00
transcript: Crawford. And we're back for another edition of TuneIn. Thanks for joining us. I'm Rick Crawford, and it is a pleasure to have you. We are talking about the politics of spending here in Congress and how that affects your tax dollars. And it's the beginning of the year. This is the time of year when we start talking about the annual appropriations process. Why I'm bringing this up now is because we're going to start it much, much earlier this year than we ever had before. But let me give you a little bit of background here before we go any further. And you know, and you've heard me say many times that the process here in Washington, it's been screwed up for a long time, long before I ever got here. But it's supposed to be a little bit different this year, so let's get into that. Every year, as we've talked about before, the House Budget Committee drafts a budget, and the key purpose is to basically set the total level of spending and discretionary spending. Once the budget committee sets that total level of discretionary spending, that's known as 302A allocation, just some jargon up here that we use to classify or to give you a little bit of a nomenclature there that the appropriators can go by the 302 allocation, then the appropriations committee cuts up the pie. Now, you remember last year we had Representative Steve Womack on, who represents Arkansas, third district, and he is an appropriator. So he gave us a really good idea of what the appropriations process consists of, and we really kind of came to the best analogy is we're just cutting up that spending pie based on these 302A allocations. So the spending is supposed to be cut up, as I said, and bills are reviewed by each member and their staff, and then we pass those individually out of the house. Twelve appropriations bills. That sounds good in theory, but we all know that theory almost never matches up with reality in the past several years that's certainly been the case. So budgets are created and politics get in the way and the appropriations process can be derailed by a political topic that is not even relevant, doesn't have anything to do with the process at hand. Now I'll give you an example. Last year we started the appropriations process very early on in the year. We were making great progress. I think we got into the sixth appropriations bill and it was early on. It's still in June if I recall and then we had this dust up with the Confederate flag. And someone introduced a bill to ban the use of the display of the Confederate flag on federal property and so on. And this is frustrating because we learned my office did some research and we learned that that was already settled law. There was no need for it. And yet we allowed that kind of theatrical display to derail our appropriations process. So then we get into the governed by crisis mode. And we failed to pass the appropriations bill. Leadership then gets together and they negotiate with the White House to create one great big omnibus bill or a great big mess, if you will. I voted against it. This thing hits the floor at the 11th hour and the Branksman ship that Congress has known for. And I'm not saying that I'm a member of Congress and I'm not saying that to malign the institution. But the reality is we have to stop the governed by crisis mode that takes place here. And I think we can, but we just need to make sure that we start like we're doing this year earlier. And we can avoid these kinds of last-minute deals. I vote against these deals. And you know that. I voted against this one last year. And in the previous year, we have the CR omnibus or the chromibus. It's just chock full of junk. We don't get an adequate time to review it. And the further along you go with each turn of the page, you see that it's worse. Every page gets worse. So what are we going to do different this year? Well, we've got a new speaker at the house, as you know, and he has pledged that he will depart from that governed by crisis model. We've talked about regular order, what it means. It means different things to different people. But for him, it means getting these appropriations bills done in a timely fashion and completing that process because it's not just enough. to pass a budget and call it good, because we never stick to that anyway. The budget is the guideline for the appropriations process. Now, you know that I vote against budgets because there's no fundamental underpinning that it creates any sort of binding result there that we get off of those numbers quickly and easily, and that's the whole problem with the flawed budget process, and we've talked about that before. this year speaker ryan he's had time to start from scratch plan the whole thing uh... from the beginning and he didn't interview background christmas time with bill bennett describing that process take a listen
